claim: Infertility affects 15% of couples.
source: Infertility is a common clinical problem affecting 15% of couples; ovulatory disorders account for 25% of this total (Macaluso et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Macaluso et al., 2010

claim: Ovulatory disorders account for 25% of infertility cases.
source: Infertility is a common clinical problem affecting 15% of couples; ovulatory disorders account for 25% of this total (Macaluso et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Macaluso et al., 2010

claim: Malfunction of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis can cause ovulatory dysfunction and/or other disturbances of the reproductive cycle.
source: The hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis controls reproduction and malfunction of this axis can cause ovulatory dysfunction and/or other disturbances of the reproductive cycle (Helm et al., 2009; Plant and Zeleznik, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Helm et al., 2009 and Plant and Zeleznik, 2015

claim: GnRH neurons form the final common pathway for central neural regulation of reproduction.
source: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons form the final common pathway for central neural regulation of reproduction.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about the reproductive neuroendocrine system

claim: GnRH stimulates the pituitary to secrete follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone (LH).
source: GnRH stimulates the pituitary to secrete follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone (LH), which regulate gonadal steroid and gamete production.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about the reproductive neuroendocrine system

claim: Follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone regulate gonadal steroid and gamete production.
source: GnRH stimulates the pituitary to secrete follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone (LH), which regulate gonadal steroid and gamete production.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about the reproductive neuroendocrine system

claim: Estradiol, via estrogen receptor alpha (ERα), plays crucial roles in both homeostatic negative feedback and positive feedback action on GnRH/LH release in females.
source: Estradiol, via estrogen receptor alpha (ERα), plays crucial roles in both homeostatic negative feedback and positive feedback action on GnRH/LH release in females (Döcke and Dörner, 1965; Moenter et al., 1990; Lubahn et al., 1993; Krege et al., 1998; Wintermantel et al., 2006; Christian et al., 2008; Glanowska et al., 2012; Cheong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Low estradiol levels suppress pulsatile GnRH/LH release.
source: Low estradiol levels suppress pulsatile GnRH/LH release, whereas sustained elevations in estradiol during the late follicular phase of the cycle cause a switch of estradiol feedback action from negative to positive, inducing prolonged GnRH/LH surges, which ultimately triggers ovulation (Christian and Moenter, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Christian and Moenter, 2010

claim: Sustained elevations in estradiol during the late follicular phase of the cycle cause a switch of estradiol feedback action from negative to positive.
source: Low estradiol levels suppress pulsatile GnRH/LH release, whereas sustained elevations in estradiol during the late follicular phase of the cycle cause a switch of estradiol feedback action from negative to positive, inducing prolonged GnRH/LH surges, which ultimately triggers ovulation (Christian and Moenter, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Christian and Moenter, 2010

claim: Sustained elevations in estradiol induce prolonged GnRH/LH surges, which ultimately trigger ovulation.
source: Low estradiol levels suppress pulsatile GnRH/LH release, whereas sustained elevations in estradiol during the late follicular phase of the cycle cause a switch of estradiol feedback action from negative to positive, inducing prolonged GnRH/LH surges, which ultimately triggers ovulation (Christian and Moenter, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Christian and Moenter, 2010

claim: GnRH neurons typically do not express detectable ERα.
source: As GnRH neurons typically do not express detectable ERα (Hrabovszky et al., 2001), estradiol feedback is likely transmitted to GnRH neurons by ERα-expressing afferents.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hrabovszky et al., 2001

claim: Estradiol feedback is likely transmitted to GnRH neurons by ERα-expressing afferents.
source: As GnRH neurons typically do not express detectable ERα (Hrabovszky et al., 2001), estradiol feedback is likely transmitted to GnRH neurons by ERα-expressing afferents.
evidence: Logical inference based on the lack of ERα expression in GnRH neurons

claim: Kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate and anteroventral periventricular (AVPV) regions are estradiol-sensitive GnRH afferents.
source: Kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate and anteroventral periventricular (AVPV) regions are estradiolsensitive GnRH afferents that are postulated to mediate estradiol negative and positive feedback, respectively (Oakley et al., 2009; Lehman et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Oakley et al., 2009 and Lehman et al., 2010

claim: Arcuate kisspeptin neurons are postulated to mediate estradiol negative feedback.
source: Kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate and anteroventral periventricular (AVPV) regions are estradiolsensitive GnRH afferents that are postulated to mediate estradiol negative and positive feedback, respectively (Oakley et al., 2009; Lehman et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Oakley et al., 2009 and Lehman et al., 2010

claim: AVPV kisspeptin neurons are postulated to mediate estradiol positive feedback.
source: Kisspeptin neurons in the arcuate and anteroventral periventricular (AVPV) regions are estradiolsensitive GnRH afferents that are postulated to mediate estradiol negative and positive feedback, respectively (Oakley et al., 2009; Lehman et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Oakley et al., 2009 and Lehman et al., 2010

claim: Kisspeptin potently stimulates GnRH neurons.
source: Kisspeptin potently stimulates GnRH neurons and Kiss1 mRNA is differentially regulated in these nuclei by estradiol (Han et al., 2005; Messager et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2005; Pielecka-Fortuna et al., 2008; Lehman et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2015; Yip et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Kiss1 mRNA is differentially regulated in arcuate and AVPV nuclei by estradiol.
source: Kisspeptin potently stimulates GnRH neurons and Kiss1 mRNA is differentially regulated in these nuclei by estradiol (Han et al., 2005; Messager et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2005; Pielecka-Fortuna et al., 2008; Lehman et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2015; Yip et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: ERα in kisspeptin cells is critical for estradiol negative and positive feedback.
source: ERα in kisspeptin cells is critical for estradiol negative and positive feedback, as kisspeptin-specific ERα knockout (KERKO) mice exhibit higher frequency LH pulses and fail to exhibit estradiol-induced LH surges (Mayer et al., 2010; Dubois et al., 2015; Greenwald-Yarnell et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and evidence from KERKO mice

claim: Kisspeptin-specific ERα knockout (KERKO) mice exhibit higher frequency LH pulses.
source: ERα in kisspeptin cells is critical for estradiol negative and positive feedback, as kisspeptin-specific ERα knockout (KERKO) mice exhibit higher frequency LH pulses and fail to exhibit estradiol-induced LH surges (Mayer et al., 2010; Dubois et al., 2015; Greenwald-Yarnell et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Kisspeptin-specific ERα knockout (KERKO) mice fail to exhibit estradiol-induced LH surges.
source: ERα in kisspeptin cells is critical for estradiol negative and positive feedback, as kisspeptin-specific ERα knockout (KERKO) mice exhibit higher frequency LH pulses and fail to exhibit estradiol-induced LH surges (Mayer et al., 2010; Dubois et al., 2015; Greenwald-Yarnell et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: In KERKO mice, ERα is deleted as soon as Kiss1 is expressed, before birth in arcuate kisspeptin neurons.
source: First, ERα is deleted as soon as Kiss1 is expressed, before birth in arcuate kisspeptin neurons (also called KNDy neurons for coexpression of kisspeptin, neurokinin B and dynorphin) and before puberty in AVPV kisspeptin neurons (Semaan et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Semaan et al., 2010 and Kumar et al., 2014

claim: In KERKO mice, ERα is deleted before puberty in AVPV kisspeptin neurons.
source: First, ERα is deleted as soon as Kiss1 is expressed, before birth in arcuate kisspeptin neurons (also called KNDy neurons for coexpression of kisspeptin, neurokinin B and dynorphin) and before puberty in AVPV kisspeptin neurons (Semaan et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Semaan et al., 2010 and Kumar et al., 2014

claim: Arcuate kisspeptin neurons are also called KNDy neurons for coexpression of kisspeptin, neurokinin B and dynorphin.
source: First, ERα is deleted as soon as Kiss1 is expressed, before birth in arcuate kisspeptin neurons (also called KNDy neurons for coexpression of kisspeptin, neurokinin B and dynorphin) and before puberty in AVPV kisspeptin neurons (Semaan et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: Established nomenclature in the field

claim: Early deletion of ERα in KERKO mice may cause developmental changes in kisspeptin cells and/or their networks.
source: This may cause developmental changes in these cells and/or their networks.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential consequences of early ERα deletion

claim: In KERKO mice, ERα is deleted from all kisspeptin cells, making it impossible to assess independently the role of AVPV and arcuate kisspeptin neurons.
source: Second, ERα is deleted from all kisspeptin cells, thus making it impossible to assess independently the role of AVPV and arcuate kisspeptin neurons.
evidence: Logical inference about the limitations of the KERKO model

claim: Combining CRISPR-Cas9 with targeted viral vector injection allows deletion of ERα in a nucleus-specific and temporally-controlled manner.
source: Combining CRISPR-Cas9 with targeted viral vector injection allows deletion of ERα in a nucleus-specific and temporally-controlled manner to address the above caveats (Swiech et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Swiech et al., 2015

claim: The firing frequency of AVPV kisspeptin neurons was lower in ovary-intact KERKO mice compared to controls.
source: The firing frequency of AVPV kisspeptin neurons was lower in ovary-intact KERKO mice compared to controls (Figure 1a,b, two-way ANOVA/Holm-Sidak, p=0.0001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a,b with statistical analysis

claim: OVX reduced firing rate in AVPV kisspeptin cells from control mice.
source: OVX reduced and estradiol treatment increased firing rate in cells from control, but not KERKO, mice (Figure 1a,b two-way ANOVA/Holm-Sidak, control intact vs OVX p=0.009, intact vs OVX + E, p=0.02, OVX vs OVX + E, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a,b with statistical analysis

claim: Estradiol treatment increased firing rate in AVPV kisspeptin cells from control mice.
source: OVX reduced and estradiol treatment increased firing rate in cells from control, but not KERKO, mice (Figure 1a,b two-way ANOVA/Holm-Sidak, control intact vs OVX p=0.009, intact vs OVX + E, p=0.02, OVX vs OVX + E, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a,b with statistical analysis

claim: The firing rate of AVPV kisspeptin neurons in KERKO mice does not respond to circulating estradiol.
source: OVX reduced and estradiol treatment increased firing rate in cells from control, but not KERKO, mice (Figure 1a,b two-way ANOVA/Holm-Sidak, control intact vs OVX p=0.009, intact vs OVX + E, p=0.02, OVX vs OVX + E, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a,b with statistical analysis

claim: The firing frequency is higher in cells from OVX + E control than OVX + E KERKO mice.
source: As a result of this difference, the firing frequency is higher in cells from OVX + E control than OVX + E KERKO mice (p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: AVPV kisspeptin neurons in control mice exhibit a greater number of depolarization-induced bursts (DIB) and rebound bursts when estradiol is elevated.
source: AVPV kisspeptin neurons in control mice mice exhibit a greater number of depolarization-induced bursts (DIB) and rebound bursts when estradiol is elevated, confirming previous observations (Wang et al., 2016) (Figure 1c,d,e, Chi-square, DIB, p=0.02; rebound, p=0.02; Fisher's exact post hoc test, DIB, OVX vs OVX +E, p=0.008, rebound OVX vs OVX +E p=0.03, for other paired comparisons, p>0.2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c,d,e with statistical analysis and citation to Wang et al., 2016

claim: In KERKO mice, depolarization-induced bursts and rebound bursts were rare (<25% of cells) in all steroid conditions tested and were not regulated by estradiol.
source: In KERKO mice, these two types of bursts were rare (<25% of cells) in all steroid conditions tested and were not regulated by estradiol (Figure 1c,d,e, Chi-square, DIB, p=0.4, rebound, p=0.3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c,d,e with statistical analysis

claim: Cells from ovary-intact KERKO mice generated fewer action potentials compared to controls in response to current injection.
source: Cells from ovary-intact KERKO mice generated fewer action potentials compared to controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Action potential generation as a function of current injection was similar in cells from OVX control and OVX KERKO mice.
source: Action potential generation as a function of current injection was similar in cells from OVX control and OVX KERKO mice but was increased by estradiol only in control mice (Figure 1f, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA/Holm-Sidak, intact, 20 pA, p=0.03, 30 pA, p=0.06; OVX +E, 20 pA to 50 pA, p≤0.04).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f with statistical analysis

claim: Action potential generation was increased by estradiol only in control mice, not in KERKO mice.
source: Action potential generation as a function of current injection was similar in cells from OVX control and OVX KERKO mice but was increased by estradiol only in control mice (Figure 1f, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA/Holm-Sidak, intact, 20 pA, p=0.03, 30 pA, p=0.06; OVX +E, 20 pA to 50 pA, p≤0.04).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f with statistical analysis

claim: Reduced action potential firing of AVPV kisspeptin neurons from KERKO mice may be attributable at least in part to decreased input resistance compared to controls.
source: Reduced action potential firing of AVPV kisspeptin neurons from KERKO mice may be attributable at least in part to decreased input resistance compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, two-way ANOVA/Holm-Sidak control vs KERKO, intact, p=0.006, OVX, p=0.7, OVX +E p=0.02).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis

claim: Both depolarization-induced bursts and rebound bursts are sensitive to NiCl (100 µM) at levels that fairly specifically block T-type calcium channels.
source: As both depolarization-induced bursts and rebound bursts are sensitive to NiCl (100 µM) (Lee et al., 1999) at levels that fairly specifically block T-type calcium channels, we measured T-type (IT) current density and voltage dependence.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 1999

claim: IT current density was decreased in AVPV kisspeptin cells from gonad-intact KERKO mice compared to controls.
source: IT current density was decreased in AVPV kisspeptin cells from gonad-intact KERKO mice compared to controls (Figure 2a,b, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA/Holm-Sidak, −50 mV, p=0.003; −40 mV, p=0.002; −30 mV, p=0.003).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a,b with statistical analysis

claim: The voltage dependence of activation of IT was not different between control and KERKO groups.
source: The voltage dependence of activation was not different between groups, but the voltage dependence of inactivation was depolarized in cells from KERKO mice (Figure 2c, control vs KERKO, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, V1/2 activation −52.2 ± 1.6 vs −48.6 ± 1.4 mV, p>0.1; slope 5.5 ± 0.6 vs 5.5 ± 0.7, p>0.1; V1/2 inactivation −74.8 ± 4.1 vs −61.9 ± 3.1 mV, p=0.03; slope −3.1 ± 0.5 vs −4.2 ± 0.3, p=0.1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c with statistical analysis

claim: The voltage dependence of inactivation of IT was depolarized in cells from KERKO mice.
source: The voltage dependence of activation was not different between groups, but the voltage dependence of inactivation was depolarized in cells from KERKO mice (Figure 2c, control vs KERKO, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, V1/2 activation −52.2 ± 1.6 vs −48.6 ± 1.4 mV, p>0.1; slope 5.5 ± 0.6 vs 5.5 ± 0.7, p>0.1; V1/2 inactivation −74.8 ± 4.1 vs −61.9 ± 3.1 mV, p=0.03; slope −3.1 ± 0.5 vs −4.2 ± 0.3, p=0.1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c with statistical analysis

claim: Two sgRNAs were designed that target exon1 of Esr1 based on software prediction.
source: Two sgRNAs were designed that target exon1 of Esr1 based on software prediction (Ran et al., 2013); sites predicted by FengZhang's guide design software (http://crispr.mit.edu) as possible off-target regions for binding of these guides are listed in Table 3.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ran et al., 2013 and reference to software tool

claim: Cells expressing either of the sgRNAs targeting Esr1, but not lacZ, exhibited a peak-on-peak sequencing pattern, indicating disruption of the gene.
source: Cells expressing either of the sgRNAs targeting Esr1, but not lacZ, exhibited a peak-on-peak sequencing pattern, indicating disruption of the gene (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a

claim: The infection rate for AVPV-AAV-Esr1 was 81 ± 4%.
source: The infection rate for AVPV-AAV-Esr1 was 81 ± 4% (Figure 3d, Esr1-guide 1 [g1] 82 ± 2%, n = 3; Esr1-guide 2 [g2] 81 ± 8%, n = 3) and only 28 ± 1% of AVPV kisspeptin cells expressed ERα post infection (Figure 3d, n = 3, Esr1-guide1 27 ± 0.4%; n = 3, Esr1-guide2 28 ± 2%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d

claim: Only 28 ± 1% of AVPV kisspeptin cells expressed ERα post infection with AVPV-AAV-Esr1.
source: The infection rate for AVPV-AAV-Esr1 was 81 ± 4% (Figure 3d, Esr1-guide 1 [g1] 82 ± 2%, n = 3; Esr1-guide 2 [g2] 81 ± 8%, n = 3) and only 28 ± 1% of AVPV kisspeptin cells expressed ERα post infection (Figure 3d, n = 3, Esr1-guide1 27 ± 0.4%; n = 3, Esr1-guide2 28 ± 2%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d

claim: In mice that received AVPV-AAV-lacZ, the infection rate was comparable at 82 ± 2%.
source: In mice that received AVPV-AAV-lacZ (n = 3), the infection rate was comparable at 82 ± 2%, but there was no disruption of ERα; 72 ± 2% of AVPV kisspeptin neurons expressed ERα, which is similar to control mice (Kumar et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Kumar et al., 2015

claim: In mice that received AVPV-AAV-lacZ, 72 ± 2% of AVPV kisspeptin neurons expressed ERα, which is similar to control mice.
source: In mice that received AVPV-AAV-lacZ (n = 3), the infection rate was comparable at 82 ± 2%, but there was no disruption of ERα; 72 ± 2% of AVPV kisspeptin neurons expressed ERα, which is similar to control mice (Kumar et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Kumar et al., 2015

claim: The ERα antibody used recognizes the C-terminus.
source: Of note, the ERα antibody used recognizes the C-terminus, suggesting a lack of rare splice variants that were generated at low levels in initial ERKO mice (Couse et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Couse et al., 1995

claim: Neither AVPV-AAV-Esr1 guide (tested independently) nor the AVPV-AAV-lacZ disrupted reproductive cyclicity.
source: Neither AVPV-AAV-Esr1 guide (tested independently) nor the AVPV-AAV-lacZ disrupted reproductive cyclicity (Figure 3e), even in mice with a high rate of bilateral infection (~80%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e

claim: Mice with AVPV-AAV-Esr1 or AVPV-AAV-lacZ entered proestrus at the same frequency in the last four weeks compared to the first four weeks.
source: These mice entered proestrus at the same frequency in the last four weeks compared to the first four weeks (two weeks pre-surgery plus the first two weeks post-surgery, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA/Holm-Sidak, before vs after; g1, n = 3, 1.3 ± 0.1 vs 1.6 ± 0.1; g2, n = 4, 1.2 ± 0.1 1.4 ± 0.1; lacZ n = 4, 1.3 ± 0.2 vs 1.3±0.1, p>0.1 for each paired comparison).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: Both proestrous and estradiol-induced LH surges were blunted after ERα knockdown in AVPV kisspeptin neurons.
source: Both proestrous and estradiol-induced LH surges were blunted after ERα knockdown (Figure 3f,g, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA/Holm-Sidak; f, lacZ, 3pm vs 5pm, p=0.04; lacZ vs Esr1, 4pm, p=0.006, 5pm, p<0.0001, h, lacZ AM vs PM, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f,g with statistical analysis

claim: There were fewer corpora lutea in mice with Esr1 guides targeted to the AVPV.
source: There were fewer corpra lutea (CL) in mice with Esr1 guides targeted to the AVPV (p<0.05, guides 1 and 2 combined n = 6, 5.2 ± 2.1 CL/mouse, vs lacZ guide n = 5, 10.8 ± 0.4 CL/mouse, two-tailed paired Student's t test with Welch's correction, t = 2.598, df = 5.305).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: Ovulation is disrupted in a substantial subpopulation of AVPV-AAV-Esr1 mice but can proceed with the blunted LH surge in some animals.
source: This suggests ovulation is disrupted in a substantial subpopulation of these mice but can proceed with the blunted LH surge in some animals.
evidence: Inference based on the variation in corpora lutea counts

claim: Cells not infected with AVPV-AAV-Esr1 and cells infected with either AVPV-AAV-Esr1 guide but in which ERα protein was detected exhibited similar firing signatures in terms of DIB and rebound bursts.
source: Cells not infected with AVPV-AAV-Esr1 and cells infected with either AVPV-AAV-Esr1 guide but in which ERα protein was detected exhibited similar firing signatures in terms of DIB and rebound bursts (Figure 4b,e,f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b,e,f

claim: Cells infected by AVPV-AAV-Esr1 that had undetectable ERα protein had reduced burst firing compared to AVPV-AAV-lacZ or uninfected groups.
source: In contrast, cells infected by AVPV-AAV-Esr1 that had undetectable ERα protein had reduced burst firing compared to AVPV-AAV-lacZ or uninfected groups (Figure 4e,f, Chi-square, DIB, p=0.008, rebound bursts, p=0.0008; Fisher's exact post hoc test, DIB, Esr1 vs lacZ, or vs uninfected, p≤0.03; rebound, Esr1 vs lacZ, or vs uninfected p≤0.04; for other paired comparisons, p>0.5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e,f with statistical analysis

claim: The firing signature of AAV-Esr1-infected cells with successful deletion of ERα was comparable to cells from KERKO mice.
source: The firing signature of AAV-Esr1-infected cells with successful deletion of ERα was comparable to cells from KERKO mice (Chi-square, p>0.9 for both DIB and rebound bursts).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: Cells that lost detectable ERα after AVPV-AAV-Esr1 infection produced fewer action potentials with current injection than cells infected with AAV-lacZ.
source: Cells that lost detectable ERα after AVPV-AAV-Esr1 infection also produced fewer action potentials with current injection than cells infected with AAV-lacZ (Figure 4d left and center, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA/Holm-Sidak, Esr1 vs lacZ, 20 pA, p=0.08; 30 to 50 pA p≤0.02).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d with statistical analysis

claim: Loss of ERα in AVPV kisspeptin neurons led to decreased action potential rate of rise, a trend toward prolonged full-width half-maximum (FWHM), and hyperpolarized afterhyperpolarization potential (AHP).
source: Specifically, loss of ERα led to decreased action potential rate of rise, a trend toward prolonged full-width half-maximum (FWHM), and hyperpolarized afterhyperpolarization potential (AHP) (Figure 4–j, two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test, h, p=0.02, j, p=0.0002; i, Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.06).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4h-j with statistical analysis

claim: A lower percent of AVPV-AAV-Esr1 knockdown cells express Kiss1 mRNA.
source: Single-cell PCR analysis also indicates that a lower percent of AVPV-AAV-Esr1 knockdown cells express Kiss1 and a trend to increase in Esr2 mRNA (AVPV-AAV-Esr1, 23 cells from four mice; AVPV-AAV-lacZ, 16 cells from three mice; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: There is a trend to increase in Esr2 mRNA in AVPV-AAV-Esr1 knockdown cells.
source: Single-cell PCR analysis also indicates that a lower percent of AVPV-AAV-Esr1 knockdown cells express Kiss1 and a trend to increase in Esr2 mRNA (AVPV-AAV-Esr1, 23 cells from four mice; AVPV-AAV-lacZ, 16 cells from three mice; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Expression of the mRNA for progesterone receptor (Pgr) did not differ between AVPV-AAV-Esr1 and AVPV-AAV-lacZ groups.
source: Interestingly, expression of the mRNA for progesterone receptor (Pgr) did not differ between groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting the estradiol-dependence of this gene may be paracrine regulated in the brain as in other tissues (Hilton et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to Hilton et al., 2015

claim: The estradiol-dependence of progesterone receptor gene may be paracrine regulated in the brain as in other tissues.
source: Interestingly, expression of the mRNA for progesterone receptor (Pgr) did not differ between groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting the estradiol-dependence of this gene may be paracrine regulated in the brain as in other tissues (Hilton et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on data and citation to Hilton et al., 2015

claim: The infection rate for Arc-AAV-Esr1 was 92 ± 3%.
source: The infection rate for Arc-AAV-Esr1 was 92 ± 3% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, n = 3 Esr1-guide1 96 ± 2%; n = 3 Esr1-guide2 86 ± 2%) and only 34 ± 3% of KNDy neurons expressed ERα post infection (Figure 5a n = 3 Esr1-g1, 38 ± 0.3%; n = 3 Esr1-g2, 30 ± 5%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5a

claim: Only 34 ± 3% of KNDy neurons expressed ERα post infection with Arc-AAV-Esr1.
source: The infection rate for Arc-AAV-Esr1 was 92 ± 3% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, n = 3 Esr1-guide1 96 ± 2%; n = 3 Esr1-guide2 86 ± 2%) and only 34 ± 3% of KNDy neurons expressed ERα post infection (Figure 5a n = 3 Esr1-g1, 38 ± 0.3%; n = 3 Esr1-g2, 30 ± 5%).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a

claim: In mice that received Arc-AAV-lacZ, the infection rate was comparable (94 ± 3%), and 92 ± 1% of KNDy neurons expressed ERα, similar to control mice.
source: In mice that received Arc-AAV-lacZ, the infection rate was comparable (Figure 5a n = 3, 94 ± 3%), and 92 ± 1% of KNDy neurons expressed ERα, similar to control mice (Kumar et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a and citation to Kumar et al., 2015

claim: Mice with Arc-AAV-Esr1 targeted to the arcuate began exhibiting disrupted cyclicity three to four weeks post surgery.
source: In contrast to mice with Arc-AAV-Esr1 targeted to the AVPV region, mice with the same virus targeted to the arcuate began exhibiting disrupted cyclicity three to four weeks post surgery (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b

claim: Mice with Arc-AAV-Esr1 entered proestrus less frequently after surgery than before.
source: These mice entered proestrus less frequently after surgery than before (two weeks pre-surgery plus the first two weeks post-surgery, Figure 5d, two-way repeated-measures ANOVA/Holm-Sidak, g1, p=0.002, g2, p=0.03).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d with statistical analysis

claim: There was no difference in LH pulse frequency measured on the day of estrus between Arc-AAV-Esr1 vs Arc-AAV-lacZ injected mice.
source: There was no difference in LH pulse frequency measured on the day of estrus or mean levels between Arc-AAV-Esr1 vs Arc-AAV-lacZ injected mice on estrus (Figure 5c,e,f).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5c,e,f

claim: LH response to kisspeptin and to GnRH was reduced in Arc-AAV-Esr1 mice.
source: Notably, LH response to kisspeptin and to GnRH was reduced in Arc-AAV-Esr1 mice (Figure 5g, two-way repeated measures ANOVA/Holm-Sidak, lacZ, control vs kisspeptin or GnRH, p<0.001; Esr1 vs lacZ for kisspeptin and GnRH both, p≤0.002).
